name: Ahinoam (Saul's wife)
title: King Saul's wife
summary: Ahinoam, daughter of Ahimaaz, was the wife of Saul – the first king anointed over Israel. Her name appears in the genealogy in 1 Samuel 14:49–50, where Saul's immediate family is listed: his sons Jonathan, Ishvi and Malkishua, and his daughters Merab and Michal. The biblical sources give no information about actions, statements or initiatives from Ahinoam herself, and she appears solely through her connection to Saul's household. Nevertheless, her role as mother places her at the center of several pivotal events in the early monarchy: Jonathan's strong bond with David, Michal's marriage to David, and Merab's role in Saul's political alliances. Ahinoam illustrates how many women in the biblical royal narratives are visible primarily through their family relationships rather than through their own actions.

keyEvents.title: Mentioned in Saul's genealogy
keyEvents.description: In a summary of Saul's family and closest circle, Ahinoam daughter of Ahimaaz is mentioned as his wife. The text lists the sons Jonathan, Ishvi, and Malchishua; the daughters Merab and Mical; as well as the commander Abner son of Ner.

versions.summary: Ahinoam was the daughter of Ahimaaz and wife to King Saul, Israel's first king. She was the mother of several of Saul's children, including Jonathan, Ishvi, Malchishua, and Michal. As Saul's wife, she was Israel's first queen, although the Bible gives little information about her life and role.
versions.title: Israel's First Queen
versions.reason: [minor] The title 'Israel's first queen' is somewhat speculative. The Bible never uses the title 'queen' for Ahinoam, and it is unclear whether she held a formal queenly role. A more neutral title could be 'King Saul's wife'.; [minor] The role 'queen' is somewhat imprecise. The Bible never refers to her as queen. The term 'wife' or 'royal wife' is more accurate based on the biblical text.; [major] In 1 Sam 14:49, the sons Jonathan, Jisjvi, and Malkishua are mentioned, along with the daughters Merab and Michal. However, it is worth noting that Saul also had a son named Ishbosheth (Eshbaal), who became king after Saul (2 Sam 2:8). Whether Ahinoam was his mother is uncertain, but he should be considered. Additionally, 'Jisjvi' is correct, but it should be clarified that some scholars regard this as a variant of the name Ishbosheth. The list also fails to explicitly distinguish between sons and daughters in the data model, so the names should be carefully checked.; [minor] The summary mentions that she was the mother of 'several of Saul's children, including Jonathan, Jisjvi, Malkishua, and Michal,' but omits Merab, who is also named as Saul's daughter in 1 Sam 14:49. Merab should be included in the summary.; [minor] The three key events are all based on the same verse (1 Sam 14:49-51). 'Mother of Jonathan' and 'Mother of Michal' are not actually separate events but deductions from the same passage. Consider merging them or rephrasing to something more informative.; [major] Footnotes that could enrich the profile are missing. There are interesting linguistic, historical, and theological points worth including.

versions.summary: Ahinoam was the daughter of Ahimaaz and wife to King Saul, Israel's first king. She is mentioned in 1 Samuel as the mother of Saul's sons Jonathan, Ishvi, and Malchishua, as well as his daughters Merab and Michal. The Bible provides very little information about her life and role beyond this. As the wife of Israel's first king, she held a unique position in Israel's history, but the text attributes no independent action or influence to her.

versions.reason: [minor] The two key events overlap significantly. Both refer to 1 Sam 14:49-51 and both concern Ahinoam being mentioned as Saul's wife and mother of his children. It would have been more effective to merge them into a single event, or at least make them more distinct.; [minor] The phrasing resembles the earlier version (v1) quite closely. It is recommended to vary word choice and structure more to avoid repetition. The text could also be enriched with slightly more contextual information.; [minor] The Bible text in 1 Sam 14:49 mentions only three sons (Jonathan, Ishvi, and Malchishua) and two daughters (Merab and Michal). Saul also had a son named Ish-bosheth (Eshbaal), mentioned in 2 Sam 2:8. It can be debated whether Ishvi and Ish-bosheth are the same person, but it is worth considering whether Ish-bosheth/Eshbaal should be included.; [minor] Saul also had a son named Abinadab (1 Sam 31:2; 1 Chr 8:33; 9:39), who fell together with Jonathan and Malchishua on Mount Gilboa. Consider including him in the list of children.

versions.summary: Ahinoam, daughter of Ahimaaz, was married to Saul, the first king over Israel. She is mentioned in 1 Samuel 14:49–50 in an overview of Saul's family, where she is linked to his sons Jonathan, Ishvi, and Malkishua, and his daughters Merab and Michal. Despite her position as wife to Israel's first monarch, the biblical texts provide very limited information about her as a person. She is credited with no direct actions or statements, but through her children she became indirectly connected to decisive events in the early monarchy – including Jonathan's deep friendship with David and Michal's marriage to him.
versions.title: King Saul's wife
versions.reason: [minor] The list of Saul's sons in 1 Sam 14:49 mentions three sons, but Saul also had a son named Ish-bosheth (Eshbaal) who played an important role after Saul's death. A comment on this is already found in the footnotes, but it may be considered whether the list should include him – possibly with a note that he might be identical to Jishvi.; [minor] The verses referred to include verse 51, but Ahinoam is specifically mentioned in verse 50. Verse 51 concerns Abner and Saul's family line. It is not wrong to include it as context, but strictly speaking, verses 49–50 are the most relevant for Ahinoam.

footnotes.text: The name Ahinoam (אֲחִינֹעַם) means 'my brother is grace' or 'brother of beauty.' It is composed of the Hebrew words 'ach' (brother) and 'no'am' (grace, beauty).

There are two women named Ahinoam in the Bible: Saul's wife (1 Sam 14:50) and Ahinoam from Jezreel, who became one of David's wives (1 Sam 25:43). Some scholars have speculated whether these might be the same person, which would imply that David took over Saul's wife. However, most scholars regard them as two different women.

The term 'queen' was rarely used for a king's wife in ancient Israel. Instead, it was often the king's mother (gebirah) who held the most prominent female role at court. Ahinoam is mentioned only as Saul's wife, without any formal title.
Ahinoam's father Ahimaaz is not the same Ahimaaz mentioned as Zadok's son and messenger during Absalom's rebellion (2 Sam 15:27). The name was common in ancient Israel.

In 1 Sam 14:49, three of Saul's sons are named, but Chronicles (1 Chr 8:33; 9:39) lists four sons: Jonathan, Malchishua, Abinadab, and Eshbaal (Ish-bosheth). It is possible that Ishvi is another name for either Abinadab or Eshbaal, but this remains debated among scholars.

The genealogy in 1 Sam 14:49–51 serves as a literary conclusion to the section on Saul's wars and military organization. It is a common feature in Deuteronomistic history to summarize a king's family and circle in connection with his reign.
